routes.description: Establish that classical theism offers a coherent and comparatively adequate explanation of central features of reality and withstands the principal objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more independent theistic inferences remain reasonable under the relevant alternatives and suffering is not shown logically incompatible with classical theism.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving explanatory case and the coherence of classical theism to the intellectual reasonableness of personal theistic belief.

centralBridges.description: Show that the universe's contingent existence, beginning, or life-permitting conditions warrant a transcendent or intelligent explanation.
Show that intentional minds and objective moral obligations fit a personal divine foundation better than the proposed naturalistic account.
Show that omnipotence and perfect goodness can coexist with suffering when freedom and morally sufficient purposes constrain feasible worlds.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend explanatory power and other theoretical virtues as rational evidential standards alongside novel prediction.
Support a specifically historical inference to divine action from the evidence offered concerning Jesus's resurrection.

routes.description: Establish that the proposed theistic explanations lack sufficient evidential or conceptual support and that classical divine attributes conflict with the observed extent of suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the central theistic inferences have viable naturalistic alternatives or defective premises and classical theism cannot coherently account for severe suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential shortcomings and the unresolved problem of suffering to the conclusion that belief in classical theism is not intellectually reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Provide naturalistic causal or evolutionary alternatives that block the claimed necessity of divine explanations.
Show that invoking God lacks predictive or informative explanatory content sufficient to support the proposed inferences.
Show that an omnipotent and wholly benevolent God is incompatible with severe suffering absent a coherent necessity or greater-good account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge whether ancient testimony can discriminate resurrection from unreliable or analogous miracle claims.
Challenge divine-command and divine-nature accounts as foundations for objective moral standards.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin and Causal Explanation
sections.rationale: The need for an explanation of the universe and the status of quantum counterexamples determine whether a central inference to a transcendent personal cause can proceed.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Explanatory Standards
sections.rationale: The comparative treatment of design, chance, physical necessity, and predictive power governs whether cosmic fine-tuning provides rational support for theism.

sections.title: Intentionality and Scientific Naturalism
sections.rationale: Whether naturalism can coherently account for intentional thought and whether science entails the disputed philosophical consequences bears on the comparative reasonableness of the two worldviews.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The debate over whether objective value and obligation require God supplies an independent route to theism and a central naturalistic challenge to that route.

sections.title: Resurrection and Testimonial Evidence
sections.rationale: The reliability and comparative force of the offered historical evidence determine whether the specifically Christian resurrection inference contributes to the case for God.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Freedom, and Suffering
sections.rationale: The compatibility of extensive human and animal suffering with omnipotence and perfect goodness directly controls whether classical theism remains coherent and reasonable.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A contingent universe with a finite beginning is best explained by a transcendent, immaterial, personal creator.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening statement remains attributed to him throughout this span.

response.rationale: Constructive case directly advancing a central cosmic-explanation bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Clear constructive contact, though the personal-cause bridge is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but the move compresses the shift from explanation and beginning to a personal creator.

calibrationFindings.rationale: “Pretty strong evidence” recognizes evidential force, but the excerpt does not fully warrant the personal-creator conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contingency and beginning inferences are intelligible, but the decisive bridge to a personal cause remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The finite-beginning claim is asserted as strongly evidenced without representative support or developed rival comparison in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly advances the central cosmic-explanation requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is handled in this constructive excerpt.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly moves from contingency and a finite beginning to a transcendent personal explanation, while leaving that final bridge compressed.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by design than by physical necessity or chance.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Craig's explicitly introduced and uninterrupted opening statement, with numbered transitions identifying his arguments.

response.rationale: Constructive comparative argument for design over necessity and chance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies and begins comparing the principal alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is clear, though the relevant probability space and independence claim are not qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical treatment of necessity and chance outruns the compressed support.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning may result from physical necessity or chance rather than design.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt asserts independence from laws and low odds but does not develop the probability measure or strongest chance model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative structure is coherent, with one material bridge from eliminating rivals to preferring design.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Independence and improbability are asserted without representative support or a developed chance model.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly addresses life-permitting conditions and intelligent explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The main rivals are named fairly, but their strongest qualifications are omitted.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares necessity, chance, and design, arguing that constants are independent of laws and chance is extremely improbable.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The evident existence of intentional mental states conflicts with materialist atheism's denial of aboutness while fitting a worldview grounded in a divine mind.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig remains the named speaker in his continuous opening statement, and the passage explicitly discusses Rosenberg from Craig's opposing perspective.

response.rationale: Constructive comparative claim connecting intentional minds to a divine-mind worldview.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly states the reductio and the proposed theistic fit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Intentionality is identifiable, but “atheism” and Rosenberg’s particular materialism are treated too interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The first-person example pressures Rosenberg’s account but does not by itself reduce atheism generally to absurdity.

charity.alternative: Apparent aboutness may be explained causally without intrinsic intentional content.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt relies on the evident character of thought and does not address a causal-information reconstruction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-application objection is intelligible, but the move shifts from Rosenberg’s view to atheism generally and from compatibility to explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is primarily an introspective example and a compatibility contrast, without comparative explanatory support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly advances the central human-reality bridge concerning intentional minds.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately identifies denial of intrinsic intentionality but does not engage the strongest replacement account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig invokes his own thought about Rosenberg as a reductio and contrasts it with the unsurprising existence of finite minds under theism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, with values grounded in God and duties grounded in divine commands.
moves.attributionBasis: The numbered sixth argument appears in the uninterrupted opening statement that the moderator expressly assigned to William Lane Craig.

response.rationale: Constructive moral-grounding inference tied directly to the human-reality bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The values-and-duties distinction and divine grounds are explicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Values and duties are distinguished, but “objective” and the necessity of divine grounding remain compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that atheism lacks grounding is stronger than the excerpt’s support and does not compare secular accounts.

charity.alternative: Objective morality may have a non-divine foundation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt asserts that atheism lacks resources without assessing alternative realist ethical theories.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is structurally clear, but the conditional that objective morality requires God is not defended here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central exclusion of non-divine grounds is asserted rather than comparatively supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly addresses objective obligations and a personal divine foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opposing position is reduced to nihilism despite live non-theistic alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds values in God and duties in commands, then asserts that atheism lacks comparable explanatory resources.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' transformed belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection, which entails God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: This numbered seventh argument remains within Craig's explicitly introduced opening statement and uses his characteristic first-person argumentative framing.

response.rationale: Constructive historical inference supporting the subsidiary resurrection bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies three proposed facts and an inference to resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical claim is clear, but “majority of historians” and “best explained” lack scope and comparison details.

calibrationFindings.rationale: “I believe” is qualified, though the historical consensus and best-explanation claims remain under-supported.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but the bridge from the listed facts to a divine miracle is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt relies on an asserted historian majority and begins listing facts without documentation or serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct support for the subsidiary historical-case bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive excerpt does not meaningfully assess a rival historical account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig identifies an empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief as three facts allegedly best explained by resurrection.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Pervasive quantum indeterminacy supplies events without sufficient causes and therefore challenges the causal principle used in cosmological arguments.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Rosenberg the floor at event 432, and his continuous opening statement includes direct references to Craig's argument here.

components.text: The causal premise behind the inference from a finite beginning to a transcendent cause.

response.rationale: The uranium-decay example directly challenges universal causal sufficiency, though it does not address contingency or the personal-cause inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive causal premise but only partially answers the multi-part cosmic case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The example is clear, but “no cause whatsoever” conflates absence of a determining cause with all causal explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Quantum mechanics is presented as certainly establishing total causelessness despite interpretive qualifications.

charity.alternative: The cosmological premise may concern things beginning from nothing, not indeterministic transitions within an existing physical system.
charity.decisiveQualification: Uranium decay occurs in a pre-existing atom and does not establish emergence of a universe from nothing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample has a coherent form, but its relevance to cosmic origination depends on an unstated equivalence between domains.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete radioactive-decay example is supplied, but the interpretation as absolutely causeless is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct attack on the causal requirement in the central cosmic bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply pressures causal determinism but omits the decisive domain distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg contrasts indistinguishable uranium atoms and infers from spontaneous alpha decay that no cause explains the difference.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: The Euthyphro dilemma and alternative ethical theories challenge the claim that objective morality depends on or uniquely indicates God.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg remains the uninterrupted speaker after his explicit introduction, and he directly names and criticizes Craig's objective-values argument.

components.text: The inference that divine commands or God uniquely ground objective moral rightness.

response.rationale: It identifies the missing account of what makes divine commands right and notes competing ethical theories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly identifies the grounding gap and its defeating consequence for uniqueness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden-shifting challenge and availability of alternatives are plainly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move challenges sufficiency and uniqueness rather than claiming that every divine account fails.

charity.alternative: God’s nature rather than arbitrary commands may constitute the good.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt raises what about God supplies rightness but does not distinguish divine-nature from voluntarist accounts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic challenge coherently exposes an explanatory regress or missing ground, with a bounded omission concerning divine nature.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual dilemma and existence of alternatives support underdetermination, though the alternatives are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the subsidiary moral-grounding challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest divine-nature response is live but not expressly handled.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg asks what about God makes imposed norms right and invokes multiple alternative ethical theories.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Ancient resurrection testimony is insufficiently reliable to justify a divine miracle, especially when comparable testimony for other religious claims is rejected.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Rosenberg's uninterrupted opening statement and expressly turns to rebut Craig's New Testament argument.

components.text: Whether testimonial evidence discriminates resurrection from unreliable or analogous religious miracle claims.

response.rationale: The Mormon, Islamic, and Scientology analogies directly challenge testimonial discrimination, but do not individually analyze Craig’s three facts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive reliability demand while leaving the particular historical evidence largely unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy is clear, but the asserted comparability of different testimonial records is not qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogies justify caution but do not by themselves show equal evidential quality.

charity.alternative: The resurrection case may rest on independently assessed historical facts rather than bare religious certification.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply does not compare source independence, dating, or the specific three-fact evidential structure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity argument is coherent, though its force depends on an undeveloped evidential analogy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific counterexamples are named, but their evidential comparability to the resurrection materials is not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct support for the subsidiary testimonial challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It raises a serious symmetry challenge but compresses the strongest historical distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg compares resurrection belief with Mormon certificates, Muhammad’s ascent, and Scientology claims rejected by the audience.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Extensive suffering is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and benevolent God because such a being would eliminate suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is still the continuously identified speaker, and he explicitly formulates the argument from evil while anticipating Craig's response.

response.rationale: Constructive incompatibility argument supporting the central evil bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly states the divine attributes and the proposed contradiction with suffering.

precisionFindings.rationale: “Benevolent” and “eliminates suffering” lack conditions concerning greater goods, freedom, or feasibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Logical incompatibility requires excluding morally sufficient reasons, which the excerpt does not do.

charity.alternative: A benevolent omnipotent being may permit suffering for freedom or a morally sufficient greater good.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not exclude such reasons or show them logically impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The simple syllogism depends on an unsupported universal conditional that benevolence eliminates all suffering.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence and seriousness of suffering are salient, but the logical necessity claim lacks the required exclusion argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the central evil-incompatibility bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument omits the decisive qualification to its benevolence premise.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg argues that an omnipotent benevolent being eliminates suffering and presents observed suffering as logically incompatible with God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The logical problem of evil requires excluding the possibility that God has morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly announces Craig's rebuttal immediately before this passage, and Craig directly addresses Rosenberg throughout the continuous span.

components.text: The unargued premise that no possible morally sufficient reason could justify divine permission of suffering.

response.rationale: It explicitly identifies what a logical incompatibility proof must establish and states that the original argument has not established it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly isolates the decisive modal burden and its consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely limits itself to defeating the logical version of the problem.

calibrationFindings.rationale: For a logical disproof, impossibility of sufficient reasons is indeed a necessary step.

charity.alternative: Observed suffering may still provide a probabilistic evidential argument against God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defeating logical incompatibility does not defeat an evidential problem of evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It correctly identifies the missing modal premise and limits the defeating consequence to logical disproof.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant follows from the logical burden; the appeal to broad rejection is secondary and not essential.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct attack on the central evil-incompatibility bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly confines its conclusion to the logical version, preserving the alternative evidential issue.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that Rosenberg must show it impossible for God to have morally sufficient reasons before logical disproof can proceed.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Metaphysical naturalism conflicts with reason and experience by denying intentionality, meaning, freedom, persistence, and persons.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Craig's explicitly framed rebuttal and maintains his first-person argumentative voice throughout.

components.text: The availability of non-divine ethical theories and the grounding challenge to divine morality.

response.rationale: The move presents contrary material against Rosenberg’s naturalism but does not answer the earlier Euthyphro or alternative-grounding demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing worldview criticism, but the selected earlier moral challenge remains substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The target shifts among Rosenberg’s metaphysical naturalism, naturalism generally, and atheism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Certainty about one’s own existence pressures a no-persons thesis but does not establish the broad rejection of naturalism without further premises.

charity.alternative: Naturalism may reconstruct persons and meaning without treating them as irreducible intrinsic properties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt treats Rosenberg’s eliminativism as exhaustive of metaphysical naturalism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cogito-style contradiction is coherent against denial of persons, but the generalization to naturalism is under-supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person experience supports the narrow objection, while the additional claims about meaning, freedom, and persistence remain largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the claim that intentional human reality fits naturalism poorly.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reductio is forceful against the quoted eliminativism but overgeneralizes to naturalism.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig contrasts Rosenberg’s denial of persons and first-person perspectives with the certainty of his own existence, then generalizes to metaphysical naturalism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Quantum-vacuum events do not establish emergence from nothing, and their causelessness remains disputed, so they do not defeat a causal inference from an absolute cosmic beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces Rosenberg's response and answers it continuously in the established rebuttal turn.

components.text: The claim that quantum events constitute uncaused beginnings relevantly analogous to cosmic emergence from nothing.

response.rationale: It identifies the pre-existing quantum vacuum and disputed interpretation as reasons the proposed counterexample does not defeat the cosmic inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts both the domain analogy and the alleged settled causelessness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between nothing and a physical vacuum, plus interpretive uncertainty, is clearly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately says causelessness is unclear rather than impossible.

charity.alternative: Indeterministic quantum transitions may still undermine a universal sufficient-cause principle.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such transitions occur within a structured physical state and their interpretation remains disputed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The domain distinction and interpretive underdetermination coherently block the asserted counterexample.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vacuum distinction is concrete and deterministic interpretations are identified, though not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct attack on a proposed central naturalistic causal alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest quantum challenge is identified and answered with both relevant qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig distinguishes a quantum vacuum from nothing and notes deterministic interpretations of quantum mechanics.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Atheism and the disputed philosophical doctrines are parallel implications attributed to science, so rejecting those doctrines does not logically refute atheism.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is explicitly introduced at the start of the turn and identifies his own book and its argumentative structure.

components.text: The inference from rejecting Rosenberg’s philosophical doctrines to rejecting atheism itself.

response.rationale: It expressly denies that Rosenberg’s controversial philosophical implications are necessary to atheism and states the consequence for Craig’s reductio.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly isolates the overgeneralization from one naturalistic package to atheism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among atheism, metaphysical naturalism, and disputed doctrines is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The independence point is strong, though saying the motion has practically nothing to do with the theses understates their possible evidential relevance.

charity.alternative: Craig’s reductio may target Rosenberg’s scientific naturalism rather than every form of atheism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even so, refuting Rosenberg’s additional doctrines does not logically refute atheism without a necessity bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope diagnosis is sound, with only a mild overstatement about complete irrelevance to reasonableness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction supports the diagnosis, though the claimed parallel relation to science is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly attacks the central intentional-minds inference against atheism.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the relevant distinction, with a minor omission concerning comparative worldview evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg distinguishes atheism from his controversial philosophical doctrines and denies that refuting the latter refutes the former.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Creaturely freedom limits which worlds God can actualize, and humans cannot establish that comparable goods, salvation, and knowledge of God were feasible with less evil.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Craig the floor, and Craig directly addresses Rosenberg by name and answers his final challenge.

components.text: Whether an omnipotent good God could have morally sufficient reasons tied to freedom and feasible worlds.

response.rationale: It supplies a free-world feasibility response and challenges the opponent’s ability to prove a better feasible world.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the logical compatibility demand, though it does not establish the actual truth of the proposed purposes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modal claim is clear, but “feasible” and the goods at stake are only briefly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately argues that the opponent cannot exclude possibility rather than claiming to prove God’s actual reasons.

charity.alternative: An omnipotent God might create comparably free creatures with less suffering.
charity.decisiveQualification: The opponent must show such a world was feasible while preserving the relevant goods.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The feasible-world response coherently blocks logical incompatibility, with one bounded ambiguity about the exact freedom constraint.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The modal burden supports the defensive conclusion, although the appeal to authority is not independently developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct support for the central evil-coherence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest alternative is directly stated and met at the modal burden appropriate to logical incompatibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that Rosenberg cannot prove a comparable world with less evil was feasible while retaining freedom, salvation, and knowledge of God.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Uncaused alpha decay and quantum symmetry breaking undermine the assumption that the universe's earliest state must have a sufficient cause.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is explicitly identified at the beginning of the uninterrupted rebuttal and formulates the challenge in his own voice.

components.text: The distinction between quantum events in a physical vacuum and an absolute cosmic beginning requiring a cause.
The assumption that the universe’s earliest state must have a sufficient cause.

response.rationale: The reply extends the quantum analogy to cosmic symmetry breaking, but does not resolve the vacuum-versus-nothing distinction or interpretive dispute.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the causal demand and cosmic application while leaving the decisive domain objection unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: “For no reason,” “without a cause,” and an explanation by quantum processes are used with insufficient distinction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Local decay and symmetry-breaking examples do not establish that an absolute earliest state lacks all sufficient explanation.

charity.alternative: Quantum processes presuppose a structured physical state and may be interpreted deterministically.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply does not answer either the ontological-domain distinction or interpretive underdetermination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogical extension is intelligible but relies on an unsupported inference from intra-universe indeterminacy to cosmic origination.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete phenomena are named, but their causelessness and relevance to an earliest state are asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct attack on the central cosmic-explanation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It restates the analogy without handling the strongest qualifications raised against it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg invokes alpha decay and quantum symmetry breaking and asks why the universe should be assumed different.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Freedom does not require catastrophic wrongdoing because God could create free agents who always choose rightly or never face suffering-producing circumstances.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument is delivered continuously by Rosenberg in his identified rebuttal, with explicit references to Craig's free-will defense.

components.text: Whether significant freedom requires agents ever to choose catastrophic wrongdoing or face suffering-producing temptation.
Whether freedom supplies a possible morally sufficient reason for the observed suffering.

response.rationale: It directly proposes free agents who always choose rightly, but does not establish that God can determine that outcome while preserving the relevant freedom.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive feasibility issue but leaves the modal compatibility of guaranteed right action and freedom unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: “Arranged” and “free will” obscure whether outcomes are guaranteed, merely foreknown, or contingently selected.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The questions establish an intuitive possibility but omit the modal constraint central to the defense.

charity.alternative: Guaranteeing that significantly free creatures always choose rightly may not be feasible for God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply does not distinguish actualizing a possible free-right world from causally arranging free choices.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed alternative is intelligible, but “arranging” guaranteed choices sits in unresolved tension with significant freedom.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The classroom analogy supports conceivability, not the modal feasibility needed to defeat the defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Direct attack on the central free-worlds coherence response.

representationalCharity.rationale: It presses a strong intuition but omits the defense’s decisive feasibility qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg asks why God could not preserve free will while withholding temptation or arranging that agents always choose rightly.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: God lacks the predictive contribution that warrants accepting theoretical entities in science and therefore does not qualify as a reasonable scientific hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Rosenberg's closing statement, and Rosenberg explicitly presents this passage as a positive argument for atheism.

components.text: Whether design has evidential explanatory content sufficient to warrant preferring it over natural alternatives.

response.rationale: The predictive criterion bears directly on warrant for design, but the move assumes prediction is the exclusive legitimate explanatory standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts evidential warrant but only partially answers the comparative fine-tuning inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move shifts from scientific predictive contribution to any explanatory or rational purpose without a stated bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Lack of novel scientific prediction does not by itself establish that a hypothesis has no explanatory warrant of any kind.

charity.alternative: A hypothesis may be supported by explanatory power, simplicity, fit, or retrodiction without unique novel predictions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt gives no reason predictive power must be the sole theoretical virtue.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from no scientific predictive contribution to no explanatory basis anywhere is overbroad.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Laplace example and general scientific practice are invoked, but exclusivity of prediction is not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Directly supports the central challenge to divine explanatory content.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move excludes a major family of evidential standards without engagement.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg invokes Laplace and argues that God contributes no predictive power to science, then infers no explanatory basis for invoking God.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Cross-cultural norms of fairness, equality, reciprocity, and cooperation can arise through natural selection because they enhanced human survival.
moves.attributionBasis: An explicit Dr. Rosenberg label introduces the answer, which remains an uninterrupted response in his characteristic first-person framing.

components.text: Whether objective moral normativity, rather than common cooperative behavior, has a non-divine ground.
Whether naturalism can explain human moral practices without theism.

response.rationale: Evolutionary cooperation explains common norms and behavior but does not contact the decisive ontological demand concerning objective rightness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It provides relevant contrary material while substituting an origins question for the grounding question.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary proposition is clear, but descriptive norms and objective normative truth are not expressly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move modestly explains how common cooperative norms could emerge rather than claiming to establish their objective truth.

charity.alternative: Evolution may explain moral beliefs and cooperation without grounding their objective correctness.
charity.decisiveQualification: The descriptive genealogy does not itself answer the normative-grounding argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evolutionary account of widespread cooperation is coherent, though it does not entail objective normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Survival value supplies a plausible mechanism, but the excerpt offers no representative evolutionary evidence or detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports a naturalistic alternative for moral behavior, though not objective moral grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply usefully reframes a nearby question but leaves the decisive objective-status qualification unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rosenberg attributes shared fairness, equality, reciprocity, and cooperation norms to survival-enhancing natural selection.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Moral values are grounded non-arbitrarily in God's essentially good character, while duties arise through commands that express that character.
moves.attributionBasis: An explicit Dr. Craig label starts the passage, and his answer continues without any intervening change of speaker.

components.text: What non-arbitrarily makes God’s commands morally right.
Whether evolutionary origins of cooperation replace an account of objective moral grounding.

response.rationale: It justifies replacing voluntarist command theory with a mainstream divine-nature account and answers the resulting grounding demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes arbitrary will from essentially good character and explains the command relation.

precisionFindings.rationale: Values, duties, divine nature, and commands are carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a coherent non-voluntarist account without claiming to prove it uniquely true.

charity.alternative: Divine commands are arbitrary exercises of will.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mainstream divine-command theory grounds goodness in God’s essential character and treats commands as expressions of that character.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual model is specific and internally supported, though its truth and uniqueness are not comparatively established.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Denying intrinsic meaning and intentionality is not self-refuting because sounds, marks, and pixels can transmit information by causally reorganizing neural circuits.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage begins with an explicit Dr. Rosenberg label and remains his uninterrupted reading and explanation until the audience applause.

components.text: The claim that denying intrinsic meaning or intentionality makes naturalistic communication self-refuting.
